$comment: Landmarks, wonders, structures and sites — the places a person can stand in. A landmark is the one kind of element where being generically true is a failure: 'a castle in Croatia' is a category with a name stuck on it. What makes Nehaj Nehaj is that it was finished in 1558 by Ivan Lenkovic out of the stone of the churches and monasteries demolished outside Senj's walls, so a besieging Ottoman force could not shelter in them. That single fact explains its date, its material, its silhouette and its politics at once. This file exists to hold that depth, and to measure where the corpus has it and where it only has a name.
$rules: Every key is an element id. A place entry for an element that does not exist is an error, and so is a landmark element with no entry.
when / who / of / site are the four facts that make a place specific rather than generic. A place carrying none of them is a category wearing a proper noun.
of is what it is MADE of, and it should name elements this corpus already has, so a landmark joins the graph rather than hanging off it. For a natural wonder, of is the rock and the process.
site answers 'why here' — the fact about the ground that explains the building. A fortress on a bare hill in cannon range of its harbour is not the same claim as a fortress somewhere in Croatia.

wanted is the global checklist and it is the whole point of the file. Coverage measured against what we happen to have is not coverage; it is a total. Measured against a world list, a corpus of European castles reports itself as one.
Regions are the UN M49 subregions, unchanged, so the denominator is somebody else's and cannot be quietly redrawn to flatter the numerator.

A place whose element name differs from its checklist line names that line in `checklist`. The claim is explicit because a matcher loose enough to pair 'Kuk Swamp' with 'Kuk Early Agricultural Site' would also pair things that are not the same place, and a coverage number is only worth having if it never counts wrongly.

$src.note: Individual places carry their own srcTitle, resolved by tools/sources.mjs like every other citation in this repository.

kinds.name: Fortification
kinds.note: Walls, castles, forts. Built against somebody, which is why they carry the clearest politics of any structure.

kinds.name: Palace or seat
kinds.note: Where power sat, as distinct from where it defended itself.

kinds.name: Monument or statue
kinds.note: Built to be looked at rather than used.

kinds.name: Engineering work
kinds.note: Bridges, aqueducts, canals, roads, dams — the structures whose purpose is entirely function.

kinds.name: Settlement or site
kinds.note: Cities, archaeological sites, whole places rather than single buildings.

kinds.name: Industrial site
kinds.note: Mines, mills, furnaces, yards. The heritage that is usually listed last and demolished first.

kinds.name: Natural wonder
kinds.note: Not built. Derives from rock, water and time — and sometimes from living things, which is what makes Plitvice a different claim from a canyon.

kinds.name: Rock art or early mark
kinds.note: The oldest deliberate marks people left on places, and the only kind of site that is global at every date.

nehaj.who: Ivan Lenković, Croatian general and captain of the Uskoks
nehaj.site: a bare hill directly above Senj, in cannon range of the harbour, with nothing left standing around it to shelter a besieging force — the churches, monasteries and houses outside the walls were demolished and their stone went into the fortress
nehaj.size: 18 m tall, 23 m wide, walls 2-3 m thick, five towers, eleven cannon openings

senj.when: inhabited over 3,000 years; a Roman municipality from 35 BC
senj.who: Iapodes, then Rome, then the Habsburg frontier
senj.site: the seaward end of the Vratnik pass, where the only easy crossing of the Velebit reaches the Adriatic

plitvice.when: still forming — the barriers grow up to 13 mm a year; national park 1949, UNESCO 1979
plitvice.who: moss and algae, which is the whole point: the dams are built by living things
plitvice.site: a karst valley where groundwater arrives saturated with calcium hydrogencarbonate; sixteen lakes drop 133 m from the first to the last

velebit.when: Mesozoic limestone, uplifted with the Dinarides
velebit.site: 145 km from Senj to the source of the Zrmanja, the seaward wall of the Dinaric karst; highest point Vaganski vrh, 1,758 m

great_pyramid.site: the Giza plateau, a limestone shelf firm enough to carry six million tonnes, west of the Nile so the river could carry the casing stone to it

colosseum.who: begun under Vespasian, finished under Titus
colosseum.site: the drained lake of Nero’s Golden House, given back to the city as a public building on the site of a private palace

great_wall.when: walls from the 7th century BC; the brick-faced wall that survives is Ming, 14th to 17th century
great_wall.site: the line where farmland gives out and steppe begins, which is why the wall follows a rainfall boundary rather than a border

forbidden_city.site: the centre of Beijing on the north-south axis, walled and moated, with every hall facing south

terracotta_army.site: a pit complex about 1.5 km east of Qin Shi Huang's tomb mound, facing the direction his conquered enemies lay

angkor_wat.site: the Angkor plain, with five to ten million sandstone blocks brought about 40 km from Mount Kulen; a moat 190 m wide and over 5 km around, and — unusually for a Khmer temple — facing west

machu_picchu.site: a ridge between two peaks above the Urubamba

ishtar_gate.site: the eighth gate of Babylon's inner wall, opening onto the processional way, so it was the first thing a visitor saw

lighthouse_of_alexandria.when: built about 280-247 BC; brought down by earthquakes between 956 and 1323
lighthouse_of_alexandria.site: the island of Pharos at the harbour mouth, on a coast so flat that a ship had no landmark to steer by without it

mausoleum_halicarnassus.site: a hillside above the harbour of Halicarnassus, visible from the sea it was meant to be admired from

colossus_of_rhodes.when: built 292-280 BC; fell in an earthquake about 226 BC, after 54 years
colossus_of_rhodes.site: the harbour of Rhodes, paid for by selling the siege equipment an unsuccessful besieger left behind

temple_of_artemis.when: the marble temple about 550 BC, burned 356 BC, rebuilt, destroyed 262 AD
temple_of_artemis.site: a marshy site near Ephesus chosen deliberately — soft ground was thought to cushion earthquakes

statue_of_zeus.site: inside the temple at Olympia, built so large for the space that Zeus would have taken the roof off if he stood up

hanging_gardens.who: attributed to Nebuchadnezzar II — and never securely located
hanging_gardens.when: described in Greek sources from the 3rd century BC onward
hanging_gardens.site: never securely located — no Babylonian text mentions them, and one reading puts them at Nineveh instead

lanse_aux_meadows.site: a landing at the northern tip of Newfoundland
lanse_aux_meadows.when: about 1021 AD, dated by a solar storm recorded in the wood

nabta_playa.site: a seasonal lakebed in the Nubian Desert
nabta_playa.when: occupied from about 9000 BCE; the stone circle around 4800 BCE
nabta_playa.who: cattle-herding people of the Nubian Desert

lalibela.when: late 12th to early 13th century, under Gebre Meskel Lalibela of the Zagwe
lalibela.site: a highland plateau of scoriaceous basalt soft enough to cut and sound enough to stand once the trenches are open

great_zimbabwe.when: built from the 11th century, the Great Enclosure 13th-15th, abandoned in the 16th or 17th
great_zimbabwe.site: granite hills that exfoliate in flat sheets under daily heating and cooling, so the building stone arrives already the right shape and needs no mortar

olduvai_gorge.when: beds spanning 1.85 million to 600,000 years ago; Zinjanthropus found July 1959, Homo habilis May 1960
olduvai_gorge.who: Homo habilis and Homo erectus, then Louis and Mary Leakey
olduvai_gorge.site: 48 km of gorge eroded up to 90 m into Pleistocene lake beds, so the sequence stands exposed in order

aksum_obelisk.when: probably carved and erected in the 4th century CE; taken by Italy in 1937, returned in three pieces in April 2005, re-erected and unveiled 4 September 2008
aksum_obelisk.who: the Kingdom of Aksum; the return cost Italy $7.7 million
aksum_obelisk.site: a stele field marking underground burial chambers — the large stelae stood over royal tombs and were carved with false windows and false doors, so the marker imitates the building the dead person no longer lives in
aksum_obelisk.size: 24 m standing, 160 tonnes, one solid block; the Great Stele beside it was 33 m and probably fell as soon as it was raised

kilwa_kisiwani.when: Great Mosque begun 1131-1170; the city's peak 13th to 15th centuries
kilwa_kisiwani.who: Swahili merchants; Husuni Kubwa built for Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman
kilwa_kisiwani.site: an island with no building stone and a harbour commanding the route to the Sofala gold

mapungubwe.site: the confluence of the Limpopo and the Shashe, on the inland end of the Indian Ocean gold route

twyfelfontein.when: engravings roughly 6,000 to 1,000 years old; UNESCO 2007
twyfelfontein.site: sandstone slabs around a spring in the Damaraland desert — the Damara name means jumping waterhole

ngorongoro.when: the volcano active 2.45 to 2 million years ago, then collapsed
ngorongoro.site: a caldera 610 m deep with a 260 km2 floor, whose rim holds grazing and water together so about 25,000 large animals stay put

uluru.when: the Mutitjulu Arkose laid down 550-530 million years ago
uluru.site: a bed of coarse arkose tipped almost vertical and left standing when the softer rock around it eroded away; 348 m above the plain, 9.4 km around, most of it still underground

budj_bim.when: one trap carbon-dated to 6,600 years; the wider system estimated up to 8,000
budj_bim.site: the Tyrendarra lava flow, which blocked the old drainage and made the wetlands the system steers

sydney_opera_house.site: Bennelong Point, a peninsula seen from three sides, which is why the roof had to work as a fifth elevation

great_barrier_reef.when: the present reef about 500,000 years old, the living veneer around 8,000
great_barrier_reef.who: coral polyps — the largest structure any living thing has built
great_barrier_reef.site: a shallow continental shelf in warm clear water, which is the only place reef-building coral can work

moai.site: Rano Raraku, one quarry of compressed volcanic ash that supplied all but 53 of more than 900 figures; 394 are still there unfinished

nan_madol.when: settled around AD 1; megalithic building from about 1180
nan_madol.site: a coral reef flat off Temwen Island, cut by tidal canals into 92 artificial islets over 1.5 by 0.5 km

skara_brae.when: occupied about 3180 to 2500 BC; uncovered by a storm in 1850
skara_brae.site: a treeless island where the only building material is flagstone, so even the beds and dressers are stone; buried in a dune until a storm took it off

newgrange.when: about 3100 BC; the solstice alignment first re-observed 21 December 1967
newgrange.who: Neolithic builders of the Boyne valley
newgrange.site: a ridge above the Boyne, oriented so the roof-box admits the midwinter sunrise down a 19 m passage; the mound is 85 m across and 12 m high

lascaux.when: 17,000 to 22,000 years old; found 12 September 1940, closed to the public 1963
lascaux.site: a sealed limestone cave in the Dordogne whose stable air preserved the pigment — and whose stability is exactly what visitors destroyed

iron_bridge.who: designed by Thomas Farnolls Pritchard, cast by Abraham Darby III
iron_bridge.site: the Severn gorge at Coalbrookdale, where the river had to be crossed and the foundry that could cast the ribs was already on the bank

wieliczka.when: documented from 1044, shaft-mined from the 13th century, sold salt until 1996
wieliczka.who: generations of miners, who carved the chapels themselves
wieliczka.site: a salt bed near Krakow, 327 m deep with 287 km of galleries

gobekli_tepe.site: a limestone ridge above the Harran plain; four enclosures excavated of about twenty, 10 to 30 m across

petra.when: Nabataean capital from the 2nd century BC, at its height in the 1st century AD with about 20,000 people
petra.site: a sandstone basin entered through the Siq, a natural cleft 3-4 m wide, watered entirely by dams, conduits and cisterns the Nabataeans built

borobudur.when: begun about 780 CE, finished about 833, under the Sailendra
borobudur.site: a hill on the Kedu Plain between volcanoes, with the Progo riverbed supplying 55,000 cubic metres of andesite; 118 m to a side, 35 m high

nazca_lines.who: the Paracas and then the Nazca
nazca_lines.site: a rainless windless plateau whose limey subsoil hardens into a crust — the only reason 1,300 km of shallow line has lasted two thousand years

djenne_mosque.when: the present building completed 1907; the first mosque here 13th-14th century
djenne_mosque.who: the masons' guild of Djenné, and the whole town every year
djenne_mosque.site: a platform 3 m above the marketplace, which is what keeps the Bani flood out of a building made of earth

citadelle_laferriere.who: Henri Christophe — at a cost of up to 20,000 lives
citadelle_laferriere.site: the 900 m summit of Bonnet à l'Évêque, several kilometres inland, so any French landing would have to climb to it; 365 cannon and stores for 5,000 men for a year

registan.site: the square at the centre of Samarkand, where proclamations were read and executions held, on the Silk Road

kuk_swamp.when: drainage from about 9,000 years ago; bananas and sugar cane by 6,900 to 6,400
kuk_swamp.site: a highland wetland at the edge of taro's range, drained by three grades of ditch; 116 hectares protected, UNESCO 2008

mohenjo_daro.when: built about 2500 BCE, abandoned about 1700 BCE; rediscovered in the 1920s
mohenjo_daro.site: the Indus floodplain — over 700 wells, one per three houses, and drains along a rectilinear grid

cahokia.when: population rose from under 3,000 to over 10,000 between 1050 and 1100; abandoned by 1400
cahokia.site: the Mississippi floodplain where maize would grow; about 120 earthworks, Monks Mound 30 m high and 622,000 cubic metres

teotihuacan.when: founded about 100 BCE, peak 350-650 CE, palaces burned about 550 CE
teotihuacan.who: unknown — the founders' origin and language are both undetermined
teotihuacan.site: a valley with obsidian nearby; an avenue 2 km long and 45 m wide, and a pyramid of over a million cubic metres

chartres.when: rebuilt 1194-1220 after a fire, re-consecrated October 1260
chartres.who: unknown masons — no architect is named
chartres.site: a hill above the Eure, on a crypt and towers that survived the fire and were built into the new church

mont_saint_michel.when: the first church from 708; the abbey built up from the 8th century onward
mont_saint_michel.who: Benedictine monks, after Aubert of Avranches
mont_saint_michel.site: a leucogranite outcrop 92 m high and 960 m around, in a bay with a 14 m tidal range — an island twice a day, and free defence the rest of the time

mbanza_kongo.when: founded about 1390, capital until the kingdom was abolished in 1915; UNESCO 2017
mbanza_kongo.who: Lukeni lua Nimi, then the kings of Kongo
mbanza_kongo.site: a mountain top at a junction of major trade routes; about 130,000 people in the city and its hinterland by the 1620s

diocletians_palace.when: begun about 295, finished by 305 when Diocletian abdicated
diocletians_palace.site: the Adriatic coast near the Brač quarries that supplied it; when Salona fell in the 7th century its refugees moved inside the walls, and about 3,000 people still live there

dubrovnik_walls.when: mainly 13th-17th centuries, the peak from the early 15th to the late 16th
dubrovnik_walls.site: a rock promontory with the sea on three sides, so the landward wall runs 4 to 6 m thick and the seaward as little as 1.5; 1,940 m around, up to 25 m high

pula_arena.when: 27 BC to AD 68, expanded under Vespasian and finished under Titus in 81
pula_arena.site: a slope outside the town walls, which carries part of the seating; 132.5 by 105.1 m, about 23,000 seats, and the only Roman amphitheatre with its whole outer ring still standing

horyuji.when: the pagoda's central pillar felled in 594; Japan's first UNESCO site, 1993
horyuji.site: the Nara basin; over 180 national treasures on one temple site, and the oldest standing wooden buildings in the world

giants_causeway.when: the lava erupted 50 to 60 million years ago, in the Paleocene
giants_causeway.site: a coast cut back by the sea through the inside of a lava flow — about 40,000 columns, mostly hexagonal, the tallest around 12 m

stonehenge.when: built in stages from about 3000 BC, the sarsen circle about 2500 BC
stonehenge.who: Neolithic and Early Bronze Age builders
stonehenge.site: Salisbury Plain, with sarsens hauled about 25 km from the Marlborough Downs and bluestones some 250 km from the Preseli hills

hadrians_wall.when: begun AD 122, most of it built in about six years
hadrians_wall.who: Legio II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix — about 15,000 men
hadrians_wall.site: the narrowest part of Britain, 117 km coast to coast; a ditch in front, the Vallum behind, a milecastle every Roman mile and a turret every third

mesa_verde.when: cliff dwellings mainly 1150-1300; abandoned about 1285 after the drought of 1276-1299
mesa_verde.site: alcoves undercut where seeping water meets a shale band inside the Cliff House Sandstone — dry, shaded in summer, sunlit in winter, and out of the rain

malbork.when: built over 132 years, 1274-1406; over half destroyed in 1945, restored since 1962
malbork.site: the Nogat river on a plain with no building stone, so the order fired its own — 21 hectares inside the outer walls

chichen_itza.when: the city from about 600 CE; El Castillo in its present form 11th-13th century
chichen_itza.who: the Maya of the northern Yucatán
chichen_itza.site: four cenotes in one place, on a peninsula whose limestone drains every river underground — the water is the reason the city is here

sigiriya.site: a granite inselberg 180 m above the plain, with one stair up through a gateway built as a lion, and water gardens at the foot that run on gravity

hagia_sophia.when: built 532-537; the dome rebuilt after collapse in 558. Church to 1453, mosque to 1935, museum to 2020, mosque since
hagia_sophia.who: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus
hagia_sophia.site: the first hill of Constantinople above the Bosphorus, on an active fault — which is why the first dome came down and the second was built steeper

sacsayhuaman.when: built in the 15th century under the Inca
sacsayhuaman.who: Inca masons — Cieza de León reports 20,000 men
sacsayhuaman.site: the ridge above Cusco, with the stone hauled about 35 km from Rumicolca; three terrace walls, the longest about 400 m and 6 m high

eiffel_tower.when: built 28 January 1887 to 31 March 1889, opened 15 May 1889
eiffel_tower.site: the Champ de Mars for the 1889 exposition; 330 m tall on a 125 m square base, and it moves 9 cm in wind and 18 cm away from the sun

himeji.when: a fort from 1333, the present castle 1601-1609; restored 2010-2015
himeji.site: a hill over the road west from the capital; 83 buildings, and a path to the keep 325 m long where the straight line is 130

pont_du_gard.when: about 40-60 AD, roughly fifteen years to build
pont_du_gard.site: the narrowest crossing of the Gardon on a 50 km line that had to fall one metre in three thousand the whole way

potala.when: begun 1645; the shell in three years, the interior in forty-five
potala.site: Marpo Ri hill at about 3,700 m on a seismic fault — 400 m east to west, 119 m high, walls battered inward and tied with copper in the foundations

benin_moat.when: from as early as 800 AD into the modern era; the Inner City Iya about 1460
benin_moat.who: the Edo, ward by ward and village by village, later under the Ogiso kings and Obas such as Oguola and Ewuare
benin_moat.site: the flat forest country around Benin City, where there is no stone to build with and no hill to build on — so the defence is dug rather than raised, and the material is the ground itself
benin_moat.size: the Inner City Iya about 12 km; the combined earthworks of Edo State estimated at some 16,000 km over about 6,500 km², with drops of up to 17 m from rampart top to ditch floor

merv.when: Achaemenid through Timurid; possibly the world's largest city by 1150; sacked by the Mongols in 1221
merv.who: four dynasties, each building beside the last rather than over it
merv.site: an oasis on the road across the Karakum where caravans had to stop; Sultan Sanjar's mausoleum is 27 m to a side and its turquoise dome was said to be visible a day's march away

ha_long_bay.when: karst developing since the Miocene, about 20 million years
ha_long_bay.site: a drowned tower-karst landscape: some 1,600 islands of Carboniferous and Permian limestone, most towers 50 to 100 m high and about six times taller than wide, each notched by the sea at the same level

tikal.when: monumental building from the 4th century BC, at its height about 200-900, abandoned by the end of the 10th century
tikal.site: a plateau in the Petén with no river, lake or cenote — the city ran on rain caught off plastered plazas and held in reservoirs

bagan.when: 11th to 13th centuries; the 1975 earthquake damaged many and 2016 damaged nearly 400 more
bagan.who: the Pagan Empire — merit-making by whoever could afford a temple
bagan.site: a dry plain in the bend of the Irrawaddy, where more than 10,000 temples went up in two centuries and about 2,200 survive

caral.when: about 2600 to 2000 BC — 1,500 years before the Olmec
caral.who: the Norte Chico, about 3,000 people here
caral.site: the Supe valley, one of nineteen related sites; the main pyramid 150 by 110 m and 28 m high, with no battlements, no weapons and no pottery anywhere

krak_des_chevaliers.when: built out by the Hospitallers 1142-1170 and again in the 13th century; surrendered 8 April 1271
krak_des_chevaliers.site: the Homs Gap, the one easy route from the Syrian interior to the coast — which is why a garrison of 2,000 sat there

taj_mahal.site: a bend of the Yamuna at Agra, laid out on a north-south axis in bilateral symmetry, with the minarets leaning outward so a fall would take them away from the tomb

chaco_canyon.when: the major period 900 to 1150; most construction beams cut 1033-1092
chaco_canyon.site: a dry canyon with no timber at all, fed by six road systems up to 97 km long and 9 m wide, dead straight regardless of terrain, in a culture with no wheel and no draught animal

brooklyn_bridge.who: John A. Roebling, then Washington Roebling, then Emily Warren Roebling
brooklyn_bridge.site: the East River, too deep and too busy for piers in the channel; 486 m of main span, and 110 cases of decompression sickness in the caissons in four months of 1872

kizhi_pogost.when: the Transfiguration Church's altar laid 6 June 1714; the Intercession rebuilt 1764; dismantled and reassembled 1999-2014
kizhi_pogost.site: an island in Lake Onega, built from Scots pine logs about 30 cm thick and 3 to 5 m long — the restoration numbered and photographed every beam before taking it apart

saint_basils.when: built 1555-1561; a tenth chapel added 1588; the colours applied between the 1680s and 1848
saint_basils.who: ordered by Ivan IV; the architect is not securely known
saint_basils.site: the edge of Red Square, built to mark the taking of Kazan — nine chapels on one foundation rather than one church with aisles

brimstone_hill.when: guns first mounted 1689; 49 by 1736; besieged and surrendered 1782; UNESCO 1999
brimstone_hill.who: designed by British military engineers, built and maintained by enslaved Africans
brimstone_hill.site: a steeply sloping hill 972 feet above the sea, commanding the approaches to St Kitts

sterkfontein.when: the fossils 2.0 to 3.4 million years old; Mrs Ples found 1947, Little Foot 1997
sterkfontein.who: Australopithecus, then Robert Broom and Ronald Clarke
sterkfontein.site: dolomite caves that opened as shafts, so anything that fell in stayed and was cemented into breccia

old_havana.when: founded 16 November 1519; burned by a corsair 1555; first fortress begun 1558; UNESCO 1982
old_havana.who: Spanish settlers, then generations of military engineers
old_havana.site: a bay with a narrow mouth and deep water inside, where the treasure fleets gathered before the Atlantic crossing

table_mountain.when: the sandstone 450 to 510 million years old, Ordovician
table_mountain.site: a syncline over Cape Town, flat because it is a valley floor left standing; 1,084.6 m at Maclear's Beacon, and about 2,285 plant species on it

robben_island.when: a prison from the late seventeenth century until 1996; political prisoners from 1961; UNESCO 1999
robben_island.who: the Dutch, then the British, then the apartheid state
robben_island.site: a flat island in Table Bay, far enough offshore to need fewer guards than a mainland prison would

alhambra.when: begun 1238 under Muhammad I; the great campaigns under Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the 14th century; surrendered January 1492
alhambra.site: a plateau above Granada, made habitable as a palace by the Sultan's Canal — two long channels and lifting devices bringing mountain water up to it

persepolis.when: earliest remains 515 BC, under Darius I, continued by Xerxes I and Artaxerxes I; burned 330 BC
persepolis.site: a terrace of 125,000 m², partly built up and partly cut out of the mountain it backs onto

ajanta_caves.when: first phase from the 2nd century BCE; second phase possibly only 460-480 CE; rediscovered 28 April 1819
ajanta_caves.who: Buddhist communities, under Harishena in the second phase
ajanta_caves.site: a horseshoe cliff of Deccan flood basalt above the Waghora river, cut into rather than built on

leptis_magna.when: founded in the second half of the 7th century BC; rebuilt under Septimius Severus from AD 193; UNESCO 1982
leptis_magna.site: a harbour on the Tripolitanian coast; abandoned and buried under dunes, which preserved it because nothing could be quarried away that nobody could see

mogao_caves.when: from 366 AD to the 14th century; Cave 17 sealed early in the 11th century, opened 25 June 1900
mogao_caves.who: Buddhist communities, beginning with the monk Le Zun
mogao_caves.site: a cliff above an oasis 25 km from Dunhuang, where the Silk Road split to pass the Taklamakan — 46,000 m² of painted wall in nearly 500 caves

mount_fuji.when: New Fuji from about 10,000 years ago; last erupted 16 December 1707 to about 1 January 1708; UNESCO 2013
mount_fuji.site: where three tectonic plates meet south-west of Tokyo, with four volcanoes built one on top of another; 3,776 m

meroe_pyramids.when: from about 270 BC, and building went on for over 700 years
meroe_pyramids.who: the Kingdom of Kush; the largest, 30 m, is thought to have been built for the Nubian queen Amanishakheto
meroe_pyramids.site: clusters on the desert ridges east of the Nile at Meroë, closely arranged rather than spread out, so a royal cemetery reads as a field of spires
meroe_pyramids.size: 6 to 30 m tall, inclined at about 70°; over 40 of them were destroyed by Giuseppe Ferlini in the 1830s looking for treasure

catalhoyuk.when: about 7500 BC to 5600 BC, at its height around 7000 BC
catalhoyuk.who: between 600 and 800 people in an average year of the middle phase; excavated by James Mellaart 1961–65 and by Ian Hodder from 1993 to 2018
catalhoyuk.site: the Konya plain, on land good enough that people stayed two thousand years without ever laying out a street — houses were rebuilt on top of each other until the settlement stood on its own remains
catalhoyuk.size: 600–800 people, houses entered through holes in the ceiling, interiors plastered smooth, the dead buried in pits beneath the floors and hearths

segovia_aqueduct.when: Roman, around the first century AD; 2016 archaeological evidence argues for after 112 AD, under Trajan or early Hadrian, rather than the older attribution to Domitian
segovia_aqueduct.site: the valley cutting across the line from the Río Frío to the city — the arches exist only because the ground drops away, and they are tallest, 28.5 m, exactly where it drops furthest
segovia_aqueduct.size: 167 arches, 28.5 m maximum height including nearly 6 m of foundation, water brought from a source 17 km away

banaue_terraces.when: disputed — Otley Beyer put them at over 2,000 years old, and several researchers contend they were built much later
banaue_terraces.who: the ancestors of the Igorot people, working largely by hand with minimal equipment
banaue_terraces.site: a mountainside about 1,500 m above sea level, under rainforest — the forest above holds the water and the terraces below are irrigated from it, so clearing the trees would drain the fields
banaue_terraces.size: terraces climbing a whole valley side, retained by walls of stone and rammed earth fed from a main canal above each cluster

ziggurat_of_ur.when: begun about 2040 BC under Ur-Nammu and completed about 2000 BC; restored by Nabonidus in the 6th century BC and again in the 1980s
ziggurat_of_ur.who: Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur
ziggurat_of_ur.site: the flat alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia, where there is no stone and no hill — so a temple that wants height has to be built out of the mud it stands on
ziggurat_of_ur.size: about 64 m by 45 m at the base; the height is an estimate, since only the foundations survive from the Sumerian period

tiwanaku.when: founded around AD 110, at its height about AD 375–700, collapsed around AD 1000
tiwanaku.who: the Tiwanaku polity; over 10,000 people at its height
tiwanaku.site: the altiplano beside Lake Titicaca, about 70 km from La Paz and nearly four kilometres up — the lake moderates a climate that would otherwise not grow anything, which is why a city that size is there at all
tiwanaku.size: ashlar masonry; the largest block at Pumapunku is estimated at 131 tonnes and the second at about 85

longmen_grottoes.who: successive dynasties and private donors, cave by cave
longmen_grottoes.site: limestone cliffs facing each other across the Yi river south of Luoyang — soft enough to cut and sound enough to hold a roof, which is the whole requirement for rock-cut work
longmen_grottoes.size: 2,345 caves, roughly 100,000 statues from 25 mm to 17 m; the Vairocana Buddha is 17.14 m

ellora_caves.when: AD 600–1000; the Kailasa temple credited to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I, r. 756–773
ellora_caves.who: Buddhist, Hindu and Jain patrons, working the same cliff in turn
ellora_caves.site: the layered basalt of the Deccan Traps in the Charanandri Hills — flood basalt lies in thick horizontal sheets, which is what makes it possible to cut a multi-storey building downward into it without the roof of one floor being the floor of nothing
ellora_caves.size: over 100 caves, 34 open; the Kailasa temple removed about 85,000 m³ of rock, courtyard 82 m by 46 m, 30 m high

prambanan.when: built about 850 CE; collapsed in a 16th-century earthquake; main Shiva temple re-erected by 1953, the complex by 1993
prambanan.who: likely begun by Rakai Pikatan and inaugurated by King Lokapala, of the Sanjaya dynasty
prambanan.site: the Prambanan plain of central Java, in the shadow of Merapi — the same volcanism that supplies the andesite also supplies the earthquakes that have twice taken the temples down
prambanan.size: 240 structures originally, 224 of them small Pervara temples in four concentric rows; the Shiva temple 47 m tall, Brahma and Vishnu 33 m

jelling_stones.when: 10th century — the smaller raised by Gorm the Old, the larger by his son Harald Bluetooth
jelling_stones.who: Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth
jelling_stones.site: Jelling, the royal seat, between two of the largest burial mounds in Denmark — the stone is placed where the dynasty already had its dead, so a new religion is announced standing on the old one
jelling_stones.size: the larger stone is inscribed on three sides and carries a crucified Christ on one and a serpent wrapped around a lion on another; enough original paint survived to recover the colours

taputapuatea.when: possibly from about AD 1000, expanded between the 14th and 18th centuries; UNESCO 9 July 2017
taputapuatea.who: the chiefs, priests and navigators of eastern Polynesia
taputapuatea.site: Opoa on the east coast of Raiatea, at a pass in the reef — a marae people arrive at by ocean voyage has to be somewhere an ocean-going canoe can land
taputapuatea.size: a paved court 44 by 60 m with an ahu of basalt and coral at the eastern end

latte_stone.when: prehistoric Marianas; twelve at the House of Taga were still upright when George Anson sketched them in 1742
latte_stone.site: the Marianas, where a house raised clear of the ground on stone pillars survives what a house on the ground does not — rain, rot and the things that live in it
latte_stone.size: the House of Taga stones stood 4.6 m and were quarried about 1,200 m from the site; one of the twelve remains standing

el_morro.when: begun 1539, design finalised 1587, main construction from March 1589, completed 1787
el_morro.who: Spain — the 1587 design by Juan de Tejada and Bautista Antonelli
el_morro.site: the headland at the mouth of San Juan Bay, which is the only thing the fort is about: everything entering or leaving the harbour passes under it
el_morro.size: six levels, walls 5.5 to 12.2 m thick, rising 43 m from the shoreline, 28 hectares with the esplanade

head_smashed_in.when: in use at least 6,000 years ago and for some 5,500 years
head_smashed_in.who: the Blackfoot, with runners who moved the herd dressed as coyotes and wolves
head_smashed_in.site: a sandstone cliff about 300 m long at the edge of the Porcupine Hills, with grazing three kilometres west and fresh water at the foot — the drive, the kill and the camp have to be one place or the meat is lost
head_smashed_in.size: a drop of 10 to 11 m, drive lanes marked by hundreds of cairns, and bone deposits 12 m deep

gur_e_amir.when: begun 1403, completed 1404; Timur buried there in February 1405, and the tomb opened by Gerasimov on 20 June 1941
gur_e_amir.who: built for Muhammad Sultan; it holds Timur, his sons Shah Rukh and Miran Shah, his grandsons Ulugh Beg and Muhammad Sultan, and his teacher Sayyid Baraka
gur_e_amir.site: Samarkand, the seat Timur built up out of a conquered world — the mausoleum raised for his heir became his own because he died first
gur_e_amir.size: an azure fluted dome 15 m across and 12.5 m high; onyx inside, a marble stalactite cornice, and a grave marker of one block of dark green jade

lope_okanda.when: petroglyphs from around 2,000 years ago; Bantu stone axes and pottery from 3,500–2,000 years ago; UNESCO 2007
lope_okanda.who: Bantu settlers of the Ogooué valley, hilltop village by hilltop village
lope_okanda.site: the meeting of rainforest and savanna — northern grassland left over from the last ice age with forest advancing into it, and an open river valley through the middle that may have been the corridor from the coast inland
lope_okanda.size: over 1,600 petroglyphs; hilltop villages with large rubbish pits, later with iron furnaces beside them
lope_okanda.srcTitle: Ecosystem and Relict Cultural Landscape of Lopé-Okanda

roi_mata_domain.when: Roi Mata was a chiefly title from the 11th to the 17th century; the best-known holder lived around 1600. Excavated 1967, UNESCO 2008
roi_mata_domain.who: José Garanger, working from the oral tradition
roi_mata_domain.site: three places rather than one, across Efate, Lelepa and Eretoka: where he lived, where he died and where he was buried — the separation is the tradition, and the tradition is what found the grave
roi_mata_domain.size: a mass burial with more than 25 members of his retinue

zollverein.when: mining from 1851 to 23 December 1986; Shaft 12 opened 1932; coking plant to 30 June 1993; UNESCO 14 December 2001
zollverein.who: Fritz Schupp and Martin Kremmer designed Shaft 12; Schupp also the coking plant
zollverein.site: the Ruhr coalfield, where the seams are deep enough that everything above ground is there to serve one hole — which is why composing the surface buildings as architecture was an argument, not a decoration
zollverein.size: up to 12,000 tons a day at Shaft 12; 6,900 employed and 3.6 million tons in 1937; a coking plant of 192 ovens reaching up to 8,600 tons of coke a day

konark.when: about 1250 CE; the main vimana fell in 1837
konark.who: Narasingha Deva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, with Shiva Samantaraya Mahapatra overseeing the work
konark.site: the Odisha coast, facing the sunrise, which is the only orientation a chariot for the sun can have
konark.size: 24 stone wheels about 3 m across with eight spokes each, seven horses; the sanctum tower estimated at 70 m before it fell

bialowieza.when: a surviving fragment of the primeval forest of the European Plain; UNESCO 1979, extended 1992 and 2014
bialowieza.who: nobody, which is the point — and then four bison brought back from zoos in 1929
bialowieza.site: the European Plain, where the same forest once ran unbroken and everywhere else was cleared — what is left is not a park but a control sample
bialowieza.size: 1,418.85 km² inscribed; almost half the wood dead, ten times a managed forest; more than 800 European bison

amsterdam_canals.when: dug through the 17th century; the north-west sector begun 1613 and finished around 1625; UNESCO 2010
amsterdam_canals.who: the city, working to one plan across the whole breadth of the layout
amsterdam_canals.site: wet ground at the mouth of the Amstel, where a city expands by digging rather than by building outward — every new ring of canal makes the land the next ring of houses stands on
amsterdam_canals.size: over 100 km of canals, about 90 islands, 1,500 bridges and 1,550 monumental buildings

panama_canal.when: French work from 1 January 1881 to bankruptcy in 1889; American from 1904; opened 15 August 1914
panama_canal.who: France first, at a cost of about 22,000 dead and US$287,000,000; then the United States, with William C. Gorgas suppressing yellow fever and malaria — about 5,600 died in the American phase
panama_canal.site: the narrowest point between two oceans, and a continental divide too high to cut through — which is why the canal climbs rather than cuts, and why a lake had to be made to supply the climb
panama_canal.size: 82 km; three locks up and three down; Gatun Lake 26 m above sea level; about 200 million litres of fresh water per transit

sanchi_stupa.when: commissioned by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE; enlarged and cased in stone by the Shungas in the 2nd century BCE; toranas added in the 1st century BCE
sanchi_stupa.who: Ashoka, then the Shungas, then the Satavahanas — the southern gateway inscribed for King Satakarni
sanchi_stupa.site: a hill above Vidisha on the trade routes of central India — a stupa is meant to be walked around and seen from a distance, and a flat-topped hill gives it both
sanchi_stupa.size: the dome 16.46 m high and 36.6 m across; the original was about half that diameter

kalyan_minaret.who: Arslan Khan Muhammad of the Karakhanids; the architect known as the master of Bako
kalyan_minaret.site: Bukhara, on the flat of the Zarafshan oasis, where there is no stone and no high ground — so the call to prayer has to be carried by a tower and the tower has to be built of the mud underfoot, fired
kalyan_minaret.size: 45.6 m, or 48 with the point; 9 m across at the base tapering to 6 m; bricks 27 × 27 × 5 cm

carcassonne.when: Roman, then medieval; restored by Viollet-le-Duc from 1853 to 1879; UNESCO 1997
carcassonne.who: Rome, the Trencavels, the French crown — and then Viollet-le-Duc, whose restoration is itself part of what is listed
carcassonne.site: the hill above the Aude on the corridor between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, which is why there has been a fortress on it since before the walls that are there now
carcassonne.size: two concentric walls, 52 towers and barbicans, spaced to keep siege engines off the inner wall

rila_monastery.when: founded in the reign of Tsar Peter I (927–968); Hrelja's tower 1334–35; destroyed by fire 1833 and rebuilt 1834–1862; UNESCO 1983
rila_monastery.who: founded by the hermit Ivan of Rila and built by his students; rebuilt by Alexi Rilets with subscriptions from across Bulgaria
rila_monastery.site: a valley high in the Rila mountains, chosen by a hermit for being out of reach — the same remoteness later made it the one place Bulgarian script, icons and craft could carry on through five centuries of Ottoman rule
rila_monastery.size: 8,800 m² with a courtyard of 3,200 m²; 300 chambers and four chapels; frescoes finished 1846

sungbo_eredo.when: disputed — proposals range from the 10th–11th centuries to the late 14th or early 15th
sungbo_eredo.who: built in honour of the Ijebu noblewoman Oloye Bilikisu Sungbo
sungbo_eredo.site: the forest country around Ijebu Ode, where laterite hardens on exposure — so a bank cut from the ground stands, and the boundary of a kingdom can be dug instead of built
sungbo_eredo.size: more than 160 km, ringing an area about 40 km north to south, with up to 20 m from ditch floor to inner bank rim

joya_de_ceren.when: buried by the Loma Caldera eruption around AD 600; UNESCO 1993
joya_de_ceren.who: Maya farmers of the Zapotitán valley — who evacuated, so nobody is in it
joya_de_ceren.site: the Zapotitán valley 36 km north-west of San Salvador, next to a vent that opened without warning — good farmland for the same reason it was dangerous
joya_de_ceren.size: 4 to 8 m of ash in a few hours and about 10 m of pyroclastic debris in the end, cool enough to seal the village rather than burn it

monte_alban.when: founded around 500 BC, largely abandoned by about AD 900–1000
monte_alban.who: the Zapotec; population estimated at 17,200 in the Terminal Formative
monte_alban.site: a ridge top artificially levelled 400 m above the Oaxaca valley floor, at about 1,940 m — a defensible position with no water on it, which is a decision rather than a convenience
monte_alban.size: over 300 Danzantes stones recorded; Building J aligned to the rising of Capella rather than to the plaza

fasil_ghebbi.when: founded by Emperor Fasilides in 1645; UNESCO 1979
fasil_ghebbi.who: Fasilides and his successors; Fasilides' palace credited by a Yemeni ambassador in 1648 to an Indian named Abdal Kerim
fasil_ghebbi.site: Gondar, on the plateau north of Lake Tana — a permanent capital for a court that had moved with the season for centuries, which is the whole reason to build in stone at all
fasil_ghebbi.size: about 70,000 m² inside a 900 m curtain wall with twelve gates; castles of Fasilides, Iyasu I and II, Mentewab, a chancellery, a library, a banqueting hall and three churches

bikini_atoll.when: 23 devices between 1946 and 1958; the 167 islanders removed on 7 March 1946; UNESCO 3 August 2010
bikini_atoll.who: the United States; the Bikinians were moved to Rongerik, then Kwajalein, then Kili
bikini_atoll.site: a ring of reef around a lagoon far from anywhere, which is exactly why it was chosen — and the lagoon that made it a good anchorage for a target fleet is what now holds the wrecks
bikini_atoll.size: about 77 megatons in total; Castle Bravo 15 megatons and its crater still visible on the north-west cape

levuka.when: capital of the Kingdom of Fiji from 1871; Deed of Cession 10 October 1874; government moved to Suva from 1877; UNESCO June 2013
levuka.who: beachcombers, traders and then the colonial administration; Cakobau signed at Nasova
levuka.site: a strip between Beach Street and 600 m hills, many of them cliffs — the town could not grow inland, so the capital left and the buildings stayed
levuka.size: a Fijian village at the north end and Nasova at the south; the Royal Hotel from the early 1860s, Sacred Heart Church, and a town hall of 1898

sangha_trinational.country: congo, cameroon and central african republic
sangha_trinational.who: three states holding one forest between them
sangha_trinational.site: the Congo Basin, where the forest is continuous and the animals are not visible in it — the bais, natural clearings such as Dzanga Bai, are the only openings, and they are where the elephants gather
sangha_trinational.size: 7,463 km² inscribed with a buffer zone of 17,879.5 km²; Nouabalé-Ndoki, Lobéké and Dzanga-Ndoki

pantheon.site: the Campus Martius in Rome, on flat ground — a dome that large exerts its thrust outward all the way round, so it needs a site where the wall carrying it can be a complete circle
pantheon.size: 43.3 m interior diameter and the same to the oculus; the shell 6.4 m thick at the base and 1.2 m at the crown; the oculus 30 Roman feet across

parthenon.when: begun 447 BC, substantially complete by 432; the roof blown off 26 September 1687
parthenon.who: Iktinos and Callicrates, with Phidias over the sculpture
parthenon.site: the Acropolis of Athens — a limestone outcrop above the city, so the building is meant to be read from below and every refinement in it corrects for that
parthenon.size: octastyle peripteral Doric, 8 columns by 17; stylobate curvature 10.3 cm over 70 m, about 1/700; entasis around 1/550 to 1/600

knossos.when: settled from about 7000 BC; first palace about 1900 BC; destroyed about 1350 BC; reconstructed by Arthur Evans in the early 20th century
knossos.who: Minoan Crete; Evans's reinforced-concrete restoration is criticised for going past what the evidence supports
knossos.site: a low hill inland from the north coast of Crete, on ground with water — a palace that big has to be fed and drained, and the drains are among the first things you see
knossos.size: about 14,000 m²; light wells, drains, water channels, staircases and timber-reinforced multi-storey masonry

meteora.when: pillars formed after uplift about 60 million years ago; monasteries mainly from the second half of the 14th century; steps cut into the rock in the 1920s
meteora.who: Athanasios Koinovitis founded the Great Meteoron between 1356 and 1372
meteora.site: pillars of conglomerate left standing where vertical faults let the rest weather away — the point of building on them is that the only way up was a rope you controlled from the top
meteora.size: pillars over 20 m, the Varlaam cliff 373 m; 24 monasteries at the peak, six still standing and four in use

pompeii.when: buried AD 79 — a 2022 study puts the eruption at 24–25 October; identified as Pompeii by an inscription found 20 August 1763
pompeii.who: a town of 10,000 to 20,000 people; excavated by Giuseppe Fiorelli, who devised the casts
pompeii.site: the bay below Vesuvius, on soil made by the volcano that buried it — the reason the town was rich is the reason it is gone
pompeii.size: 4 to 6 m of ash and pumice, up to twelve layers of tephra and up to 6 m deep

etna.when: the first reported eruption around 1400 BCE, by Diodorus Siculus; UNESCO June 2013
etna.who: nobody — but 77 deaths are attributable with certainty to its eruptions, which is fewer than the legend
etna.site: the east coast of Sicily above a subduction zone, where silica-rich lava too sticky to run far stacks into a cone — and the soil it makes is why there are vineyards and orchards on the slopes of the thing that buries them
etna.size: 3,403 m in September 2024, and changing; sixteen eruptions in 2001 alone; the 1669 flows destroyed at least ten villages before reaching Catania

dome_of_the_rock.when: completed 72 AH, 691–2 CE; dome rebuilt 1022–3; Ottoman tiles under Suleiman, replaced 1960–2
dome_of_the_rock.who: the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik, with Raja ibn Haywa al-Kindi and Yazid ibn Sallam supervising
dome_of_the_rock.site: the Temple Mount, built around the Foundation Stone — the plan is an octagon with a circular ambulatory because the building exists to let people walk around one rock
dome_of_the_rock.size: octagon about 60 m across and 36 m high; dome about 20 m in diameter on sixteen supports; an octagonal arcade of twenty-four piers and columns

masada.when: Herod's works in the 1st century BC; the Roman siege under Lucius Flavius Silva, the wall breached 16 April, 73 AD; excavated by Yigael Yadin 1963–65
masada.who: Herod; then Silva with some 15,000 people in the siege force
masada.site: an isolated plateau over 400 m above the Judaean Desert, which is unassailable and uninhabitable for the same reason — no water — so the fortress is really the cisterns
masada.size: plateau about 550 by 270 m; a wall 4 m high and 1,300 m long; cisterns of about 40,000 m³; a Roman ramp 114 m high

cappadocia.when: ash from ancient eruptions of Erciyes, Hasan and Göllüdağ; Christian monastic use at Göreme from about 300 to 1200 AD, with frescoes from the 9th to the 11th century; UNESCO 1985
cappadocia.who: monks, and then whole towns digging downward
cappadocia.site: a landscape of soft ash capped in places by harder rock — the caps make the towers, and rock soft enough to weather into towers is soft enough to hollow out by hand
cappadocia.size: over 30 rock-cut churches and chapels at the Göreme Open Air Museum; underground cities at Derinkuyu, Kaymaklı, Gaziemir and Özkonak; 9,883.81 hectares inscribed
cappadocia.srcTitle: Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia

grand_canyon.when: the river established its course about 5 to 6 million years ago; the rock at the bottom is two billion years old
grand_canyon.who: the Colorado River, with the Colorado Plateau doing the other half of the work by rising
grand_canyon.site: a plateau that rose while a river was already running across it — uplift steepens a river without moving it, so it cuts down rather than around
grand_canyon.size: 446 km long, 6.4 to 29 km wide, over 1,857 m deep; Vishnu Schist at the bottom, Kaibab Limestone at the rim

salar_de_uyuni.when: Lake Minchin 30,000–42,000 years ago, then Tauca, then Coipasa 11,500–13,400 years ago
salar_de_uyuni.site: a closed basin on the altiplano at 3,656 m with no outlet — water arrives, and the only way it leaves is upward, so everything dissolved in it stays
salar_de_uyuni.size: about 10,582 km²; a salt crust 8 m thick; average elevation varying by less than one metre across the whole flat; brine about 0.3% lithium

urnes_stave_church.when: built about 1130, dated by dendrochronology to c. 1132, with carved parts from the later 11th century reused; UNESCO 1979
urnes_stave_church.who: owned since 1881 by the Society for the Preservation of Ancient Norwegian Monuments
urnes_stave_church.site: the Sognefjord in western Norway, wet country where a timber building set on the ground rots — which is exactly what standing it on staves is for
urnes_stave_church.size: the north portal carved with interlaced animals, snakes and vines: the last of the Viking animal styles, on a church

harappa.when: Ravi phase c. 3300–2800 BC, Kot Dijian c. 2800–2600, Mature Harappan 2600–1900, Late Harappan 1800–1300 BC
harappa.who: the Indus Valley civilisation; dug up for railway ballast around 1857
harappa.site: the Ravi flood plain, which is why the city is brick and not stone — and the same wetter climate that supported it has since become the edge of the Thar Desert
harappa.size: about 150 hectares and as many as 23,500 residents; flat-roofed brick houses, differentiated quarters, fortified centres and drainage

hoover_dam.when: begun 1931, dedicated 30 September 1935, completed 1 March 1936, more than two years early
hoover_dam.who: the United States; 112 deaths reported as associated with the construction, 96 of them on site
hoover_dam.site: Black Canyon — an arch-gravity dam needs rock walls close enough together and strong enough to take the thrust the arch hands them, which is a site condition and not a design choice
hoover_dam.size: 221.4 m high, 45 ft thick at the crest and 660 at the base; 2,480,000 m³ of concrete with 937 km of cooling pipe in it; four diversion tunnels 56 ft across; Lake Mead 112 miles long

grand_canal.when: oldest sections early 5th century BC; integrated under Emperor Yang of Sui 604–609 CE; restored by the Ming 1411–1415; UNESCO 22 June 2014
grand_canal.who: five million people on the Sui works; the Ming maintained it with about 47,004 full-time labourers and 121,500 soldiers running grain barges
grand_canal.site: the flat of the North China Plain between two river systems that run east and not north — the canal exists because the rivers go the wrong way, and it has to climb a watershed to do it
grand_canal.size: 1,776 km; summit 42 m above sea level; the pound lock invented for it by Qiao Weiyue in 984

suomenlinna.when: begun 1748 under the Swedish crown; surrendered 3 May 1808; renamed Suomenlinna 1918; UNESCO 1991
suomenlinna.site: eight islands about four kilometres south-east of Helsinki, in the approach to the harbour — the islands are the reason the fort is there and the reason its geometry had to be bent
suomenlinna.size: six of the eight islands fortified, each with its own works, and a navy dockyard at the centre

todai_ji.when: 8th century; the present Daibutsuden completed 1709; pillars remodelled with steel and concrete 1974–80
todai_ji.who: more than 2,600,000 people contributed materials or work, with 350,000 working directly on the statue
todai_ji.site: Nara, the capital when it was built — a state temple is put where the state is, and the timber to roof it had to come from a country that was already short of it by the time it burned
todai_ji.size: the hall 57 m by 50 m and 49 m high; the Buddha 14.98 m tall with a face 5.33 m across, weighing 500 tonnes

qhapaq_nan.country: colombia, ecuador, peru, bolivia, chile and argentina
qhapaq_nan.when: the Inca empire, expanding from 1438; UNESCO 2014
qhapaq_nan.who: the Inca state, and the communities along it who owed the bridges as labour
qhapaq_nan.site: the Andes, where a road built for feet and llamas rather than wheels can take stairs and switchbacks a cart could never use — so the terrain shaped the road rather than the road being cut to suit a vehicle
qhapaq_nan.size: about 40,000 km across six modern countries, serving some 12 million people; tambos a day's journey apart; one Apurímac bridge spanning 45 m on ichu-fibre cable

cologne_cathedral.when: begun 15 August 1248, halted about 1560, resumed 1842, completed 15 October 1880; reopened after war damage in 1956
cologne_cathedral.who: begun under Archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden; finished to the surviving medieval drawings
cologne_cathedral.site: the Rhine crossing at Cologne, on a pilgrimage route — a cathedral built to hold the shrine of the Magi has to be where the pilgrims already pass
cologne_cathedral.size: 157 m to the twin spires; the tallest building in the world for four years after 1880; fourteen aerial bomb hits survived

notre_dame.when: begun between 24 March and 25 April 1163, largely complete by 1260; burned 15 April 2019; reopened December 2024
notre_dame.who: Paris; the restoration cost an estimated $739 million
notre_dame.site: the Île de la Cité, the island the city started on — the cathedral stands on the oldest ground in Paris because that is where the ground was
notre_dame.size: 14th-century flying buttresses reaching fifteen metres from wall to counter-support; the flèche brought down 750 tonnes of stone and lead when it fell

yellowstone.when: eruptions 2.1 million, 1.3 million and 640,000 years ago; the first national park, 1 March 1872
yellowstone.who: signed into law by Ulysses S. Grant
yellowstone.site: a caldera 72 by 45 km over a magma chamber shallow enough to boil groundwater — every geyser in the park is that heat source finding a way out
yellowstone.size: 8,983 km²; at least 1,283 geysers recorded and about 465 active in a year, out of at least 10,000 hydrothermal features; the 640,000-year eruption threw out over 1,000 km³

iguazu_falls.when: cut into the Serra Geral basalts of the Paraná Basin; UNESCO 1984 and 1986
iguazu_falls.who: the Iguazu river, working on a layered lava pile
iguazu_falls.site: where the river crosses three stacked basalt flows — hard rock over softer means the lip holds while the rock under it is cut away, which is why the falls step rather than slope
iguazu_falls.size: about 275 drops across 2.7 km, the longest 82 m; the Devil's Throat 80–90 m wide and 70–80 m deep; average flow 1,756 m³/s, a record 45,700 on 9 June 2014

angel_falls.when: first flown over by Jimmie Angel on 16 November 1933; he landed on the tepui on 9 October 1937 and walked down in eleven days
angel_falls.who: the Churún river, and a mountain with a vertical edge
angel_falls.site: the rim of Auyán-tepui in Canaima — a table mountain ends in a cliff rather than a slope, so a river reaching the edge does not descend, it leaves
angel_falls.size: 979 m in total; an uninterrupted plunge of 807 m, then about 400 m of cascade and rapids and a final 30 m drop

seokguram.when: begun 751, completed by the Silla court in 774; cased in concrete in an early 20th-century restoration; UNESCO 1995
seokguram.who: credited to Kim Daeseong, finished shortly after his death
seokguram.site: a hillside above Bulguksa on Mount Toham — an artificial grotto put where a natural one would be, so the building has to supply what the rock would otherwise have given it
seokguram.size: a rotunda with a hemispherical ceiling of granite blocks held by stone rivets and no mortar; the Buddha 3.5 m on a 1.34 m lotus pedestal

port_arthur.when: a timber station from 1830, a penal settlement for secondary offenders from 1833 to 1877; UNESCO 31 July 2010
port_arthur.who: the British convict system, for men who had reoffended after transportation
port_arthur.site: the Tasman Peninsula, joined to the rest of Tasmania only at Eaglehawk Neck, 30 m wide — the site is the security, and the buildings only have to hold what the water already holds
port_arthur.size: the Separate Prison completed 1853 and extended 1855, cruciform so the wings can be watched from a hub; 1,646 graves on the Isle of the Dead, 180 of them marked

kakadu_rock_art.when: paintings up to 20,000 years old; occupation for at least 40,000 and possibly 65,000 years
kakadu_rock_art.who: the Aboriginal people of the Kakadu region, continuously for around 60,000 years
kakadu_rock_art.site: overhangs and shelters in the Arnhem Land escarpment — the art survives where the rock keeps the rain off it, so the galleries are exactly where people were already sheltering
kakadu_rock_art.size: more than 5,000 recorded art sites; Ubirr and Burrunguy (Nourlangie Rock) among them

tash_rabat.when: 10th or 15th century; identified by the Kyrgyz Academy of Sciences as possibly a 10th-century monastery before it was a caravanserai
tash_rabat.site: a valley at 3,200 m below a pass, where there is no timber — so every room is roofed by corbelling stone into a dome, and the light comes through the top because there is nowhere else to put a window
tash_rabat.size: 31 rooms, square, domed on squinches, of rubble stone on clay mortar with gypsum sealing the joints

larabanga_mosque.when: founded 1421 by tradition; rendered in sand and cement in the 1970s; storm damage 2002; restored in adobe 2023
larabanga_mosque.who: by legend an Islamic trader named Ayuba, told to build it in a dream
larabanga_mosque.site: the savanna of northern Ghana, where the building material is earth — which is why the form is buttresses and timbers rather than walls and windows
larabanga_mosque.size: about 8 m by 8 m, two pyramidal minarets, twelve conical buttresses tied by horizontal timbers

volubilis.when: from the 3rd century BC; peak in the late 2nd century AD; abandoned by the 11th; earthquake 1755; UNESCO 1997
volubilis.who: Mauretanian and then Roman; later quarried by Moroccan rulers for Meknes
volubilis.site: fertile agricultural country on the far edge of the empire — a colonial town that far out has to be worth the distance, and olives are what made it worth it
volubilis.size: about 42 hectares inside a 2.6 km circuit of walls; around 20,000 inhabitants; 58 oil-pressing complexes excavated

ayutthaya.when: the kingdom formally established 4 March 1351, with a substantial town there before that; the city fell 7 April 1767
ayutthaya.who: the Ayutthaya kingdom, one of the three great powers of Asia in the early 16th century
ayutthaya.site: an island in the rivers — a meander closed off by a canal on the east side makes a moat around the whole city out of water that was already there
ayutthaya.size: destroyed completely after a fourteen-month Burmese siege

baalbek.when: the Temple of Jupiter constructed in the mid-1st century and probably completed around AD 60; the largest block uncovered in 2014
baalbek.who: Rome, on a much older sanctuary
baalbek.site: the Beqaa valley, with the quarry above the temples — which is why the unmoved blocks are still there to be measured against the moved ones
baalbek.size: the largest known ancient block about 19.6 × 6 × 5.5 m, estimated 1,650 tonnes, still lying in the quarry beside the Stone of the Pregnant Woman

aral_sea.when: diversions from the early 1960s; commercial fishing gone by 1987; the Kokaral dike completed August 2005
aral_sea.who: the Soviet cotton plan — and since 2005, Kazakhstan holding the northern remnant behind a dike
aral_sea.site: an endorheic basin in the desert: a lake with no outlet, which means its size is entirely a balance between what the rivers bring and what evaporates — divert the rivers and there is no other term in the equation
aral_sea.size: 68,000 km² and the fourth-largest lake in the world in 1960; 60% of the area and 80% of the volume gone by 1998; a tenth of its original size by 2007; salinity from 10 g/L to about 30

sagrada_familia.when: begun 19 March 1882; Gaudí architect director from 28 March 1884; died 1926 with less than a quarter built; completion expected 2026
sagrada_familia.who: Antoni Gaudí, and since him a century of others working to his geometry
sagrada_familia.site: Barcelona — and deliberately one metre lower than Montjuïc, because Gaudí held that his work should not rise above the hill
sagrada_familia.size: 18 spires planned, 14 built; the Tower of Jesus Christ 172.5 m, the tallest church in the world; funded from visitor fees at about €25 million a year

hwaseong.when: 1794 to 1796; the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe published 1801
hwaseong.who: King Jeongjo of Joseon, designed by Chŏng Yagyong, built by paid workers rather than corvée
hwaseong.site: Suwon, where Jeongjo moved his father's remains — the fortress is a tomb-town, so it had to be built quickly and be worth living in
hwaseong.size: 5.74 km of wall, 4 to 6 m high; 700,000 person-hours; 870,000 nyang and 1,500 sacks of rice in wages

sundarbans.when: UNESCO listings across four protected areas; tiger counts from the 2011 India and 2015 Bangladesh surveys
sundarbans.who: nobody built it, and about 180 Bengal tigers live in it
sundarbans.site: the Ganges delta, where fresh water meets salt and the mud is airless — the whole forest is a set of answers to those two problems
sundarbans.size: 10,277 km², about 6,017 in Bangladesh and 4,260 in West Bengal; roughly 180 tigers, 106 and 74

cueva_de_las_manos.when: in several waves between 7,300 BC and AD 700; UNESCO 1999
cueva_de_las_manos.site: a rock shelter above the Pinturas river canyon — a sheltered wall is what makes 9,000 years of paint survivable
cueva_de_las_manos.size: over 2,000 handprints, 829 left to 31 right; iron oxides, natrojarosite, pyrolusite and copper oxide, with gypsum as a binder

palenque.when: about 226 BC to about 799 AD; Pakal's tomb opened by Alberto Ruz Lhuillier in 1952
palenque.who: the Maya of Palenque; less than 10% of the city has been explored
palenque.site: a shelf in the Chiapas jungle with the Otulum running across it — the stream is the reason the site works and the reason it had to be buried
palenque.size: about 2.5 km² uncovered by 2005, with more than a thousand structures still under jungle; the aqueduct over 100 m long under a 3 m corbel vault

palmyra.when: the Temple of Bel dedicated AD 32; more than 200,000 people under Zenobia around 270; levelled by Aurelian in 273; the cella destroyed by IS on 30 August 2015
palmyra.who: Palmyrene merchants with colonies along the Silk Road; Zenobia; then Aurelian, and then IS
palmyra.site: an oasis around the spring Efqa, 215 km north-east of Damascus — a caravan crossing that desert has no choice about where to stop
palmyra.size: the Great Colonnade 1.1 km long; tower and underground tombs in the Valley of the Tombs, several destroyed in September 2015

aachen_cathedral.when: begun about 796, consecrated 805; Charlemagne buried there 814; one of the first twelve UNESCO sites, 1978
aachen_cathedral.site: Aachen, chosen for its hot springs and made a capital — the chapel is the fixed point of a court that had been itinerant
aachen_cathedral.size: an inner octagon 14.46 m in diameter; thirty German kings crowned there between 936 and 1531; columns from Cologne, Rome and Ravenna

moscow_kremlin.when: oak 1339, white limestone 1366–68, the present brick walls 1485–1495; UNESCO 1990
moscow_kremlin.who: Ivan III, with Pietro Antonio Solari on the walls and towers and Marco Ruffo on the palace
moscow_kremlin.site: the hill where the Moskva meets the Neglinnaya — two rivers give two sides of a defence for nothing, and the wall only has to close the third
moscow_kremlin.size: 2,235 m of wall enclosing about 275,000 m², 5 to 19 m high and 3.5 to 6.5 m thick; twenty towers, the Troitskaya 80 m

mauna_kea.who: nobody; the summit is treated in Hawaiian tradition as the region of the gods, once open only to high-ranking aliʻi
mauna_kea.site: a dormant shield volcano whose gentle slopes put a buildable plateau at 4,207 m — above the inversion layer, so the cloud stays below it and the air above is dry, dark and still
mauna_kea.size: 4,207.3 m above sea level and 9,330 m from its base on the ocean floor; thirteen observation facilities, funded by as many as eleven countries

versailles.when: building from 1661; the Hall of Mirrors 1678–86; largely complete at Louis XIV's death in 1715; UNESCO 1979
versailles.who: Louis XIV, with Louis Le Vau and then Jules Hardouin-Mansart
versailles.site: Louis XIII's hunting lodge on marshy ground away from Paris — the site was chosen for being nowhere, because the point was to move the court out of a city that had rebelled
versailles.size: about 63,154 m² and roughly 2,300 rooms; 2,143 windows, 1,252 chimneys, 67 staircases; 815 hectares of park now, over 8,000 before the Revolution

unfinished_obelisk.when: New Kingdom; a second unfinished obelisk base found at the same site in 2005
unfinished_obelisk.who: Egyptian quarrymen, working with dolerite pounders
unfinished_obelisk.site: the granite quarries at Aswan, which is where every Egyptian granite obelisk comes from — so the failures stay where the successes started
unfinished_obelisk.size: about 41.75 m and nearly 1,090 tonnes if it had been finished, roughly a third larger than any obelisk ever raised

nok_terracotta.when: the culture from about 1500 BCE to about 1 BCE; the earliest terracottas perhaps 900 BCE; iron smelting 750–550 BCE
nok_terracotta.who: the Nok culture of central Nigeria; excavated at Taruga from 1961
nok_terracotta.site: central Nigeria — Nok village, Taruga and Samun Dukiya in Kaduna State
nok_terracotta.size: near life-size heads and bodies, hollow and coil-built, slipped and burnished, fired for several hours under grass and twigs

igbo_ukwu_bronze.when: roughly the 9th to 12th centuries; excavated by Thurstan Shaw
igbo_ukwu_bronze.who: the founders of Igbo-Ukwu; three sites on Anozie family land — Igbo Isaiah, Igbo Richard and Igbo Jonah
igbo_ukwu_bronze.site: three deposits in one village: a store of vessels and ornaments, a high-status burial with regalia and tusks, and a domestic and ritual pit — which is why the finds can be read as a society rather than as a hoard
igbo_ukwu_bronze.size: more than 150,000 glass beads with carnelian and stone, of six major glass types, much of it from Mesopotamia, Egypt or the eastern Mediterranean

kilimanjaro.who: nobody; Kibo is dormant, Mawenzi and Shira extinct
kilimanjaro.site: a free-standing mountain off a plain rather than a peak in a range — so its ice cap is fed by nothing but itself, which makes it a clean measurement of a warming climate
kilimanjaro.size: 5,895 m; three cones, Kibo, Mawenzi at 5,149 m and Shira at 4,005 m; ice cover 11.40 km² in October 1912 and under 1 km² by June 2011

niagara_falls.when: retreating since the last glaciation; erosion averaged 1–1.5 m a year over 560 years, now about 30 cm
niagara_falls.who: the Niagara river, and since the 20th century the engineers diverting it
niagara_falls.site: where the river crosses the Niagara escarpment — hard Lockport caprock over soft Rochester shale, which is the whole mechanism: undercut the soft bed and the hard cap falls
niagara_falls.size: Horseshoe Falls about 57 m high; average annual flow 2,400 m³/s, a recorded peak of 6,370

my_son.when: built between the 4th and 13th centuries; 71 temples recorded by Henri Parmentier from 1899; bombed August 1969; UNESCO 1999
my_son.site: a bowl in the hills of central Vietnam encircled by mountains — a Shaiva sanctuary placed where the landscape already makes an enclosure
my_son.size: 71 temples in 14 groups; all but one of red fired brick, with the ornament carved into the brick and no organic trace of mortar between courses

tassili.when: most of it from the ninth and tenth millennia BP; traditions from Archaic (10,000–7500 BCE) through Round Head, Pastoral and Horse to Camel (from 1000 BCE); UNESCO 1982
tassili.who: the people of a green Sahara, and then of a drying one
tassili.site: eroded sandstone rock forests with gorges and pools, and nearly 300 natural arches in the south-east — shelter and water in a place that has since become desert around them

siwa_oracle.when: inscriptions from the 4th century BCE; Alexander the Great arrived in 331 BC; the fortress damaged by three days of rain in 1926
siwa_oracle.who: the oracle of Amun, whom Herodotus says took the form of a ram here
siwa_oracle.site: the rock of Aghurmi in an oasis of about 200 springs, deep in the Libyan desert — the distance is the point of the oracle, and the aridity is why building in salt and mud works at all
siwa_oracle.size: built of kershif, salt and mud brick, with palm logs

djemila.when: built in the 1st century AD; abandoned after the fall of Rome, 5th–6th century; UNESCO 1982
djemila.who: Rome, as a military garrison in Numidia
djemila.site: a narrow triangular plateau 900 m above sea level — defensible, and too tight for the standard plan, which is exactly what makes the town worth reading
djemila.size: forum, cardo and decumanus to the standard plan; two fora, temples, basilicas, arches; the theatre outside the walls

cape_coast_castle.when: Portuguese post 1555; Swedish fort 1653; Danish 1657, Dutch 1663, English 1664; dungeons by about 1682; UNESCO 1979
cape_coast_castle.who: Sweden, Denmark, the Dutch and then the Royal African Company
cape_coast_castle.site: the surf coast of Ghana, where the fort is the last hard point before an ocean — which is why the dungeons are under the parade ground and the door out of them faces the water
cape_coast_castle.size: dungeons cut into the rock as large vaulted cellars, divided into apartments, able to hold a thousand people

manhyia_palace.when: built 1925, after the Aban palace was demolished in the War of the Golden Stool; museum opened 12 August 1995
manhyia_palace.who: built by the British; occupied by Prempeh I and Osei Agyeman Prempeh II
manhyia_palace.site: Manhyia in Kumasi, the Asante capital — a palace put back where the destroyed one stood, which is the whole political content of it
manhyia_palace.size: residence of two Asantehene; the current Asantehene lives in a newer palace beside it

drakensberg_art.when: the oldest dated wall painting about 2,400 years old, with paint chips at least a thousand years older; UNESCO 2000
drakensberg_art.site: the escarpment on the KwaZulu-Natal–Lesotho border, where hard basalt caps the soft Clarens sandstone — the sandstone weathers into overhangs and the basalt keeps them dry
drakensberg_art.size: between 35,000 and 40,000 works, the largest such collection in the world; 20,000 recorded at 500 sites; 1,146 in Sebaayeni Cave alone

lamu.when: established 1370; the economy rested on the slave trade until its abolition in 1907; UNESCO 2001
lamu.who: Swahili builders, with influences from Arabia, India and Europe
lamu.site: an island on the Swahili coast where the building materials are the reef and the creek — coral rag for walls, mangrove poles for spans, which is why the rooms are the length of a pole
lamu.size: 25,385 residents in 2019, 23 mosques, and about 3,000 donkeys instead of vehicles

dzanga_sangha.when: reserve established 1990; part of the Sangha Trinational World Heritage Site since 2012
dzanga_sangha.who: the BaAka, who work as trackers and guides, and have lived in these forests for generations
dzanga_sangha.site: Congo Basin rainforest with one clearing in it — the bai is where the mineral soil is, so it is where the elephants come out of a forest that otherwise hides them completely
dzanga_sangha.size: 6,865.54 km² of tropical rainforest; IUCN category VI

loango.who: the Kingdom of Loango, capital Buali; Vili merchants trading inland
loango.site: the coast between Cape St Catherine and the mouth of the Congo — a bay that ships could work, with copper country behind it
loango.size: exported copper from Mindouli and cloth in quantity before it exported people, and then people in considerable quantities

tsodilo.when: occupation evidence reaching back about 24,000 years; the paintings span from AD 400 or earlier to the mid-1800s; UNESCO 2001
tsodilo.who: the San, for whom it is the birthplace of all life, and the Hambukushu
tsodilo.site: four quartzite hills rising out of flat Kalahari sand about 40 km from Shakawe — visible from a great distance in country that has no other landmark, which is most of why they are sacred
tsodilo.size: over 4,500 rock paintings across some 500 archaeological sites; the highest hill 1,400 m

old_quebec.when: Champlain founded the fort and the habitation in 1608; historic district established 10 July 1963; UNESCO 3 December 1985
old_quebec.who: Samuel de Champlain, and then two empires
old_quebec.site: Cap Diamant above the narrowing of the St Lawrence — the cliff makes the position and splits the town in two, Upper and Lower
old_quebec.size: 1,400 buildings over 1.42 km²; the only walled city north of Mexico

copan.when: sixteen rulers from AD 426 to about 822; the Hieroglyphic Stairway built AD 710 and extended 755; UNESCO 1980
copan.who: the Copán dynasty, founded by K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' and ending with Ukit Took'
copan.site: a river valley in western Honduras — and the river later cut 300 m into the acropolis to a height of 37 m before it was diverted south in the 1930s
copan.size: the Hieroglyphic Stairway 21 m long, 62 steps, 2,200 glyphs — the longest known Maya text

red_fort.when: commissioned 12 May 1639, completed 6 April 1648; plundered by Nadir Shah 1739; UNESCO 2007
red_fort.who: Shah Jahan, designed by Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who also designed the Taj Mahal
red_fort.site: the Yamuna bank at Delhi — the river gives one side of the defence and the water for the channel that runs through the palaces
red_fort.size: 254.67 acres inside 2.41 km of wall, 18 m high on the river side and 33 m on the city side

anuradhapura.when: capital from 377 BCE to 1017 CE; established under Pandukabhaya (474–367 BCE); mostly destroyed and deserted after 993 CE
anuradhapura.site: the dry zone of northern Sri Lanka, which is why the tanks — Kala Wewa, Tissa Wewa, Abhaya Wewa — are as much of the city as the stupas are
anuradhapura.size: Jetavanaramaya, Ruwanwelisaya, Thuparamaya and Abhayagiri; the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, the oldest documented planted tree in the world

kronborg.when: Krogen built in the 1420s under Eric VII; rebuilt 1574–1585 by Frederick II; burned 24–25 September 1629, exterior restored by 1639; UNESCO 2000
kronborg.who: Eric VII, then Frederick II, then Christian IV rebuilding after the fire
kronborg.site: Helsingør, where the Øresund narrows to 4 km — a toll gate needs to be somewhere no ship can pass out of range
kronborg.size: only the chapel survived the 1629 fire, saved by the strength of its arches

geirangerfjord.when: cut by glaciers; UNESCO 2005 as part of the West Norwegian Fjords
geirangerfjord.who: ice, and then farmers who lived on ledges above it
geirangerfjord.site: a glacial valley cut below sea level and flooded when the ice left — steep-sided because ice cuts U-shaped valleys where rivers cut V-shaped ones
geirangerfjord.size: 15 km long and at most 1.5 km wide; the Seven Sisters, the Suitor and the Bridal Veil; abandoned farms at Skageflå, Knivsflå and Blomberg

neuschwanstein.when: foundation stone 5 September 1869; work stopped at Ludwig II's death in 1886; built 1869–1892
neuschwanstein.who: Ludwig II, from his own means and civil list rather than the Bavarian treasury
neuschwanstein.site: a crag above Hohenschwangau — chosen for the view and the seclusion, which is the opposite of why a real medieval castle stands where it does
neuschwanstein.size: about fifteen rooms finished of a planned two hundred; 6.2 million gold marks; almost 1.5 million visitors a year now

dead_sea.country: israel, jordan and the west bank
dead_sea.when: falling about a metre a year since the 1960s
dead_sea.who: nobody; the diversion of the Jordan upstream is doing it
dead_sea.site: the lowest land surface on Earth, in a rift with no outlet — water arrives and leaves only as vapour, so the salt has nowhere to go
dead_sea.size: 439.78 m below sea level in 2025, 298 m deep, 342 g/kg salinity; 1,050 km² in 1930 and 605 in 2016

erdene_zuu.when: founded 1585; destroyed 1939; preserved as a museum from 1947; active again after 1990
erdene_zuu.who: Abtai Sain Khan of the Khalkha, after meeting the 3rd Dalai Lama
erdene_zuu.site: beside the ruins of Karakorum, and built from them — the monastery is physically the previous capital, moved a few kilometres and restacked
erdene_zuu.size: a wall intended to carry 108 stupas; three small temples and the wall survived 1939

hue_citadel.when: begun 1803–04 under Gia Long, completed 1832 under Minh Mạng; the Battle of Huế 1968; UNESCO 1993
hue_citadel.who: the Nguyễn emperors, working from a Vauban model and a Beijing plan
hue_citadel.site: the Hương river, which fills the moat and which the whole complex faces — the orientation is to the river rather than to true south, unlike the Beijing model it copies
hue_citadel.size: nearly 10 km round, 6.6 m high, walls 21 m thick; three enclosures, the Imperial City 2.5 km round; 10 of 160 buildings left after 1968

sukhothai.when: the kingdom dated from 1238; the Ram Khamhaeng inscription 1292
sukhothai.site: a monsoon plain 12 km from the modern town, where the year is a flood and then a drought — so the ponds cut through the city are not ornament, they are the calendar being held still
sukhothai.size: Wat Si Sawai, Wat Phra Phai Luang and the Ta Pha Daeng shrine among the Angkorian-influenced 13th–15th century structures

prague_castle.when: begun 870 with the Church of the Virgin Mary; St Vitus begun in the 14th century and completed 28 September 1929; the third defenestration 1618
prague_castle.who: the Bohemian and then Czech state; still the president's residence
prague_castle.site: the ridge above the Vltava at Prague — high ground over a river crossing, which is why there has been a seat of government on it for eleven hundred years
