prague_castle.size: almost 70,000 m², the largest ancient castle in the world

waitangi.when: the treaty signed 6 February 1840; grounds open to the public since 1934; Te Whare Rūnanga opened 6 February 1940
waitangi.who: Māori rangatira and the British Crown, on James Busby's lawn
waitangi.site: a lawn above the Bay of Islands — the treaty has no building because it was signed in a marquee, so the ground itself is what is kept
waitangi.size: the Treaty House restored in the 1930s for the 1940 centenary; Te Whare Rūnanga carved beside it

haamonga_a_maui.when: about 1200 AD, under Tuʻitātui, the eleventh Tuʻi Tonga
haamonga_a_maui.who: Tuʻitātui, in honour of his two sons
haamonga_a_maui.site: Tongatapu, a low coral island with no quarry rock but the reef itself — which is why a trilithon here is made of coral limestone and why moving 30 to 40 tonnes of it is the whole claim
haamonga_a_maui.size: 5.2 m high, 1.4 m wide and 5.8 m long; the uprights 30–40 tonnes each; a 10 cm V cut in the lintel, read as a solstice sight since 1967 and disputed

otrar.when: the caravan executed 1218; besieged five months and taken 1219–20; Timur died there February 1405; about forty families left by the end of the 18th century
otrar.who: Inalchuq, its governor; then Genghis Khan
otrar.site: the Silk Road crossing of southern Kazakhstan, connecting China, Europe, the Middle East, Siberia and the Urals — a place caravans have to pass, which is what made it rich and what made killing one there consequential
otrar.size: perhaps 5,000–7,000 people in the 14th to 17th centuries

patan_durbar.when: most of the standing architecture 17th century; Krishna Mandir 1667, Vishwanath 1627, Taleju Bhawani 1640 rebuilt 1667, Bhimsen 1680; heavily damaged April 2015; UNESCO 1979
patan_durbar.who: Siddhi Narsingh Malla and his son Srinivasa Sukriti
patan_durbar.site: the Kathmandu valley, on a fault — which is why the square is a record of rebuilding as much as of building
patan_durbar.size: 136 bahals and 55 major temples; the Krishna Mandir with 21 golden pinnacles

trogir.when: founded 3rd century BC as Tragurion; charter 1108; attacked 1123; Venetian from 1420; UNESCO 1997
trogir.who: Greek colonists, then Rome, Hungary and Venice
trogir.site: a small island between the mainland and Čiovo, 27 km west of Split — a town that cannot spread rebuilds on its own street plan, which is why a Greek grid is still readable
trogir.size: the Cathedral of St Lawrence with Radovan's west portal, the most significant Romanesque-Gothic work in Croatia

euphrasian_basilica.when: built from 553 under Bishop Euphrasius, on a basilica of the late 4th century that itself covered earlier building; UNESCO 1997
euphrasian_basilica.who: Bishop Euphrasius, with Byzantine masters on the walls and local ones on the floors
euphrasian_basilica.site: Poreč on the Istrian coast, within reach of Ravenna — which is how Byzantine wall mosaic got to a small Adriatic town at all
euphrasian_basilica.size: the only surviving depiction of the Mother of God in an early-Christian western basilica; the 5th-century floor mosaic and an oratory fish mosaic beneath

sighisoara.when: Transylvanian Saxons invited from the mid-12th century; recorded as Castrum Sex in 1280; urban status 1367
sighisoara.who: the Saxon guilds, each responsible for its own tower
sighisoara.site: a hill above the Târnava Mare, on the Roman fort site the 1280 document still calls a six-sided camp
sighisoara.size: towers named for the Tinsmiths, Butchers, Tailors and Furriers, hollow and fitted with lifts and galleries; the Clock Tower 64 m

te_wahipounamu.who: nobody; the pounamu it is named for was worked by Māori into tools, weapons and ornament
te_wahipounamu.site: 450 km of the South Island's western coast, where the mountains rise straight out of the sea and the glaciers reach down through rainforest — the ice is what brings the greenstone within reach
te_wahipounamu.size: 2,600,000 hectares across Aoraki/Mount Cook, Fiordland, Mount Aspiring and Westland Tai Poutini; sea level to 3,724 m; about 170 takahē

auschwitz_birkenau.who: built and run by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland; preserved by Poland as evidence
auschwitz_birkenau.site: a rail junction in occupied Poland, which is the reason the camp is where it is: people could be brought there from across Europe and killed on arrival
auschwitz_birkenau.size: 20 hectares at Auschwitz I and 171 at Auschwitz II, about three kilometres apart; 1.1 million people were murdered there, 960,000 of them Jews

vigelandsparken.when: the Monolith block quarried at Halden in autumn 1927, raised 1928, carved from 1929 by three masons over fourteen years, first shown Christmas 1944
vigelandsparken.who: Gustav Vigeland, under contract to the city of Oslo
vigelandsparken.site: Frogner Park in Oslo — 45 hectares given to one sculptor, which is why the installation reads as a single argument rather than a collection
vigelandsparken.size: 212 sculptures; the Monolith 14.12 m and 121 figures from one block; the bridge 100 m by 15 m with 58 sculptures; the fountain with 60 bronze reliefs on 1,800 m² of granite mosaic

east_rennell.when: inscribed 1998; added to the List of World Heritage in Danger in 2013 over logging
east_rennell.who: nobody built it; the reef did, and then the crust lifted it
east_rennell.site: a raised coral atoll — reef that grew at sea level and was then pushed above it, so the old lagoon is now a lake and the old reef is now the shore
east_rennell.size: 37,000 hectares; Lake Tegano brackish and at sea level; 21 of 50 bird species endemic, one endemic bat, seven endemic land snails

puuhonua_o_honaunau.when: the Hale o Keawe built about 1650; national historical park from 1955, renamed 10 November 1978, spelling corrected in 2000
puuhonua_o_honaunau.who: the chiefs of Kona; Kanuha built the Hale o Keawe for his father Keaweʻīkekahialiʻiokamoku
puuhonua_o_honaunau.site: a point on the Kona coast where a wall could cut off a piece of ground completely — the refuge has to be reachable and unmistakable, because the whole institution depends on knowing exactly where the boundary is
puuhonua_o_honaunau.size: the Great Wall enclosing the puʻuhonua; the Hale o Keawe held 23 remains and was reconstructed in the 1960s
puuhonua_o_honaunau.srcTitle: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park

morne_trois_pitons.when: national park established July 1975, the first in Dominica; UNESCO 1997
morne_trois_pitons.who: the volcano under it, still working
morne_trois_pitons.site: an island still being built — fumaroles, hot springs, geysers, mud pools and coloured streams are all the same heat source finding different ways out
morne_trois_pitons.size: 68.57 km²; the mountain 1,342 m; the Boiling Lake 82–92 °C at the edge and hotter in the middle

cueva_maravillas.checklist: Taino rock art of Cueva de las Maravillas
cueva_maravillas.when: declared a national park 22 July 1997; named Cueva Jaguar in 1926 and renamed in 1949
cueva_maravillas.site: a limestone reef gone to karst, 15 km east of San Pedro de Macorís — the art survives because it is 25 m underground, where nothing weathers
cueva_maravillas.size: 472 pictographs and about 10 petroglyphs; 800 m of cave, 25 m deep, in a park of 4.5 km²

abu_simbel.when: begun about 1264 BC, about 20 years to 1244 BC; relocated by early summer 1968
abu_simbel.who: Ramesses II; the move funded half by Egypt and half by 48 other contributors
abu_simbel.site: a cliff above the Nile in Nubia, chosen so the sanctuary faces the sunrise — and then a different cliff 208 m inland and 65 m up, because Lake Nasser was going to cover the first one
abu_simbel.size: four colossi 20 m high; the sun reaches the back wall on 22 October and 22 February; 1,036 blocks cut; $41.7 million

timbuktu.when: the Djinguereber mosque built 1327 under Mansa Musa; mausoleums destroyed June 2012
timbuktu.who: Mansa Musa and the scholars of Djinguereber, Sidi Yahya and Sankore; Abdel Kader Haidara organised the removal of the manuscripts
timbuktu.site: the southern end of a trans-Saharan route, where camel caravans meet the Niger — a city at a change of transport, which is what makes it a market
timbuktu.size: salt from Taoudenni 664 km north; 25,000 students in the golden age; about 350,000 manuscripts saved

stone_town.when: 19th-century prosperity on cloves and slaves; UNESCO 2000
stone_town.who: Omani, Swahili, Indian and European traders
stone_town.site: the Zanzibar shore, where coral stone is the building material and the harbour is the business — the town is made of the reef and paid for by what crossed the water
stone_town.size: carved doors with brass studs in the Indian tradition; the Anglican cathedral built on the largest slave market on the island, its altar where the whipping post stood

taos_pueblo.who: the Taos people; about 150 living in the historic pueblo full time as of 2010
taos_pueblo.site: the Rio Pueblo de Taos below the Sangre de Cristo mountains — a settlement that has stayed in one place for a thousand years is standing on the reason it could
taos_pueblo.size: walls several feet thick, five or six storeys; electricity, running water and indoor plumbing prohibited in the old village

uxmal.when: built around 700 AD; the ballcourt dedicated 901; the Nunnery Quadrangle 900–1000; abandoned in the 13th century
uxmal.who: the Maya of the Puuc hills
uxmal.site: the Puuc hills of Yucatán, which have no rivers and no cenotes — a city there is a city that has solved storing rainwater, and everything else follows from that
uxmal.size: Puuc style: smooth low walls under ornate friezes quoting a thatched hut; the Pyramid of the Magician oval in plan across five levels

chan_chan.when: built about 850 AD; capital of Chimor 900 to 1470, when the Inca took it
chan_chan.site: the arid north coast of Peru, where it almost never rains — which is the only reason twenty square kilometres of mud brick is still standing, and why the city had to dig 15 m wells and cut canals from the Moche to live
chan_chan.size: 20 km² with a dense centre of six; ten walled ciudadelas; walls 15–18 m carved with fish, birds, waves, crabs and nets

karnak.when: begun under Senusret I (1971–1926 BC) and continued into the Ptolemaic Kingdom (305–30 BC)
karnak.who: thirty dynasties, each adding to what the last built
karnak.site: the east bank at Thebes, on the Nile — a temple that grows for nineteen centuries has to be somewhere the state stays
karnak.size: the Hypostyle Hall 5,000 m² with 134 columns in 16 rows, 122 of them 10 m and twelve 21 m, over 3 m across; architraves about 70 tonnes

bandiagara.when: Toloy, then Tellem, then Dogon from the 14th century; UNESCO 1989
bandiagara.who: the Tellem cut the cliff caves; the Dogon spread over the plateau, the escarpment and the Seno-Gondo plains
bandiagara.site: a sandstone cliff about 500 m high and 150 km long — the buildings are on the face rather than the flat because the flat floods

virunga.when: created 1925 as Albert National Park; UNESCO 1979; on the Danger list since 1994
virunga.who: rangers — 175 of them killed up to April 2018
virunga.site: the Albertine Rift, with Nyiragongo and Nyamuragira in it — the volcanoes make the altitude and the vegetation the mountain gorillas need

okavango_delta.when: the flood peaks June to August, from rain that fell in Angola in January and February; UNESCO 22 June 2014, the 1,000th site inscribed
okavango_delta.site: a tectonic trough in the Kalahari where the Okavango simply stops — an inland delta with no outlet to any sea, so everything the river carries stays
okavango_delta.size: about 11 km³ of water a year; 6,000–15,000 km², swelling to three times its permanent size at flood

statue_of_liberty.when: arrived in crates 17 June 1885; dedicated 28 October 1886
statue_of_liberty.who: Bartholdi for the sculpture, Gustave Eiffel for the frame
statue_of_liberty.site: an island in New York harbour, facing the approach — a monument meant to be the first thing seen has to be in the water rather than on the shore
statue_of_liberty.size: 46 m of copper to the torch, 93 m from the ground; skin 2.4 mm thick

cusco.who: the Inca, then Spain building on top of them
cusco.site: a valley in the Andes on a fault — which is why the difference between mortarless Inca joints and Spanish mortar is not an aesthetic question there
cusco.size: the 1650 earthquake destroyed almost all the colonial buildings; 1950 damaged more than a third of the city and exposed the Qorikancha masonry under Santo Domingo

valley_of_the_kings.when: royal burials from about 1539 BC to 1075 BC; Tutankhamun's tomb found 4 November 1922; KV64 found 2011
valley_of_the_kings.who: the pharaohs of the 18th to 20th dynasties, and the Medjay who guarded them
valley_of_the_kings.site: a valley under the peak of Al-Qurn, which is pyramid-shaped — a hidden tomb under a natural pyramid, guarded, instead of a built one that advertises itself
valley_of_the_kings.size: 65 tombs and chambers, KV1 to KV64; over 1,000 feet of limestone with marl and shale through it

osun_osogbo.when: several centuries old; restored from the 1950s by Susanne Wenger (1915–2009); UNESCO 2005
osun_osogbo.who: the Yoruba of Osogbo, and Susanne Wenger, titled Adunni Olorisha
osun_osogbo.site: the forest along the Osun river near Osogbo — one of the last of the sacred groves that once bordered every Yoruba city, and the only reason it is still forest is that it is sacred
osun_osogbo.size: 75 ha with a 47 ha buffer; a two-week festival each August with more than 700 years behind it

lake_turkana.when: UNESCO 1997; the Gibe III dam upstream now controls the Omo
lake_turkana.who: nobody; the fossils are of the people who were there before there were any
lake_turkana.site: an endorheic rift basin in desert — no outflow, so the only water loss is evaporation and the lake concentrates; the same basin has been laying down sediment over hominin bone for millions of years
lake_turkana.size: salinity 0.244%; the largest permanent desert lake and largest alkaline lake in the world; the Omo supplies 90% of the inflow

golden_gate_bridge.when: opened 27 May 1937; longest suspension span in the world until 1964; tallest suspension towers until 1993
golden_gate_bridge.site: a mile-wide strait 113 m deep at the centre, with strong swirling tides and frequent strong winds — and fog, which is why the bridge is orange
golden_gate_bridge.size: main span 1,280 m; towers 227 m above the water; each cable 27,572 strands, about 130,000 km of wire in the two

calakmul.when: the Classic period, dominated by the rivalry between Calakmul and Tikal; UNESCO 2002
calakmul.who: the Kaan or Snake dynasty; about 50,000 people at its height
calakmul.site: deep in the Petén forest of Campeche, under closed canopy — which is why a city this size and this important was mapped so late
calakmul.size: about 1,000 structures over 2 km² and 6,250 mapped over more than 20 km²; Structure 2 over 45 m on a base 120 m square; 117 stelae

torres_del_paine.when: a Miocene laccolith in Cretaceous rock, exposed by erosion and glaciation
torres_del_paine.site: Patagonia, where the wind is the climate — the towers are what is left after the softer rock above the intrusion was taken off, first by weather and then by ice
torres_del_paine.size: towers to 2,500 m, Paine Grande 2,884 m; the park about 181,414 ha; Grey Glacier 15 km long with arms 1.2 and 3.6 km wide

simien.when: lava outpourings between about 40 and 25 million years ago; UNESCO 1978; biosphere reserve 2017
simien.who: nobody; the walia ibex lives nowhere else
simien.site: an eroded shield volcano on the Ethiopian plateau — 3,000 to 3,500 m of stacked basalt with the softer parts cut out of it, leaving pinnacles
simien.size: Ras Dejen 4,550 m, the escarpment 2,000 m; 26,000 visitors in 2016

yosemite_valley.when: glaciated repeatedly over the last 30 million years; the most recent glaciation reached only as far as Bridalveil Fall
yosemite_valley.site: the western Sierra Nevada, where a glacier ran down a river valley — ice fills a valley wall to wall and cuts sideways as well as down, which a river cannot
yosemite_valley.size: about 7.5 miles long and a mile wide, floor at 4,000 feet, walls 3,000–3,500 feet; Yosemite Falls 2,425 feet

vinales.when: UNESCO 1999, as a natural and cultural landscape
vinales.who: tobacco farmers working by hand and ox, by methods several centuries old
vinales.site: a karst valley in western Cuba where the rock dissolved unevenly — towers where it resisted, flat floor where it went, and the floor is what is farmed

itchan_kala.when: the Juma mosque founded in the 10th century and rebuilt 1788–89; most of the standing city 18th–19th century; UNESCO 1990
itchan_kala.site: the last stop before the desert crossing into Iran — a walled inner city on a caravan route is a place to be safe in for one night, and everything in it is sized for that
itchan_kala.size: walls 8–10 m high, 5–6 m thick, 6,250 m round, towers every 30 m; over 50 monuments and 250 houses in 37.5 ha; the Juma mosque on 112 reused columns

leshan_buddha.when: begun 722 by the monk Hai Tong, completed by his disciples in 803 with funding from Wei Gao
leshan_buddha.who: Hai Tong, who wanted the river calmed
leshan_buddha.site: the confluence of three rivers at Leshan, which wrecked boats — the statue faces the water because it was meant to work on it, and the spoil from carving it went into the river and did
leshan_buddha.size: 71 m tall, shoulders 28 m across; hidden gutters and channels in the hair, collar, chest and behind the ears

hampi.when: Vijayanagara ruled 1336 to 1565; sacked after Talikota in 1565 and burned for six months; UNESCO 1986
hampi.site: a landscape of granite boulders on the Tungabhadra — the building material is lying on the ground already, which is why the city could be that large that fast
hampi.size: 4,187.24 ha with about 1,600 surviving monuments; the Vittala hall with 56 beams that sound different notes; probably the world's second-largest city in 1500

delphi.when: Pythian Games from 586 BC; the oracle closed by Theodosius I in 381 AD; first major excavation 1893
delphi.who: the Pythia, and the priests who turned what she said into hexameters
delphi.site: a shelf on Parnassus above a fault zone — the chasm the Pythia sat over is the reason the site is there, and what came out of it is still argued about
delphi.size: the Sacred Way lined with treasuries, the Athenian one commemorating Marathon, 490 BC

mycenae.when: the acropolis rebuilt about 1350 BC; the Lion Gate about 1250–1200 BC; Grave Circle A excavated by Schliemann
mycenae.who: Mycenaean Greece; 30,000 people at its peak
mycenae.site: a hill between two ravines commanding the Argive plain — a citadel wants a position it can see out of and nobody can walk up to
mycenae.size: blocks well over 20 tonnes and some possibly near 100; citadel and lower town 32 hectares; the Mask of Agamemnon dated more than 300 years before the Trojan War

matera.when: occupied from about 7000 BC; evacuated in the 1950s; UNESCO 1993
matera.who: its own inhabitants, until the state moved them out
matera.site: a ravine in Basilicata where the rock is soft calcarenite — you can cut a house and a cistern out of the same face, which is the only way to live somewhere with no water
matera.size: streets running over the roofs of the houses below; uninhabitable in places into the late 1980s

krakow_old_town.when: Magdeburg Rights 1257; walls demolished and the moat planted in the 19th century; UNESCO 1978, among the first sites listed
krakow_old_town.who: the city, twice — once building the wall and once converting it
krakow_old_town.site: the Vistula crossing, with the market square at the centre of the grid the 1257 charter laid out
krakow_old_town.size: the largest medieval town square of any European city; the Planty green belt on the line of the walls; the heynal played hourly from St Mary's

bruges.when: at least 46,000 people around 1350; the Zwin silting from about 1500; UNESCO 2000
bruges.who: the weavers and spinners, reckoned the best in the world in the 12th to 15th centuries
bruges.site: the head of the Zwin inlet — a sea port that is not on the sea works only while the channel does, and this one stopped
bruges.size: 410 hectares inscribed with a 168 ha buffer; a 13th-century belfry with a carillon of 47 bells; the Church of Our Lady spire 115.6 m

kinderdijk.when: the system of 19 mills built around 1740; UNESCO 1997
kinderdijk.site: the confluence of the Lek and the Noord, in a polder that keeps sinking as it drains while the river bed keeps rising — the problem gets worse the longer it is solved
kinderdijk.size: 19 monument mills, the largest concentration of old windmills in the Netherlands, pumping in stages through an intermediate reservoir

nemrut_dag.who: Antiochus I of Commagene, for himself
nemrut_dag.site: a summit at 2,150 m in the Anti-Taurus — high, remote, and covered by a heap that refills any hole dug into it
nemrut_dag.size: the tumulus 49 m high and 152 m across; seated statues 8–9 m tall on east and west terraces, all beheaded

hattusa.when: capital of the Hittite empire in two periods; destroyed about 1200 BC in the Late Bronze Age collapse; UNESCO 1986
hattusa.site: a rocky Anatolian upland with outcrops built into the defences — and the fire that ended it is what fired the archive
hattusa.size: over 6 km of wall, two skins about 3 m thick with 2 m between, 8 m in all; roughly 30,000 clay tablets recovered

ephesus.when: the Library of Celsus about AD 125; UNESCO 2015
ephesus.who: Greek, then Roman; population estimates range from 33,600 to 172,500
ephesus.site: the mouth of the Cayster — a harbour city whose river silted its own bay, so the sea is now 3 to 4 km away and the port is inland
ephesus.size: the Library about 180 m² holding nearly 12,000 scrolls; the Great Theatre seating an estimated 25,000; 662.62 ha inscribed

alta_rock_art.when: from about 5200 BC on the revised dating to about 500 BC; found in 1973; UNESCO 3 December 1985
alta_rock_art.who: hunters and fishers of the Arctic coast
alta_rock_art.site: shoreline rock at the head of the Alta fjord, still rising out of the sea after the ice — which is why the panels are now several dozen metres inland and why their height dates them
alta_rock_art.size: more than 6,000 carvings across several sites; reindeer, elk, bear, fish, boats, hunting and fishing scenes

roskilde_cathedral.when: begun about 1170, choir consecrated 1225, work continuing to 1636 and chapels added into the 1920s; UNESCO 1995
roskilde_cathedral.who: the Danish crown — the burial church of its monarchs since the 15th century
roskilde_cathedral.site: Zealand, where there is clay and no good building stone — which is the reason Gothic arrived here in brick and then spread from here
roskilde_cathedral.size: burial chapels from the 1460s to 1924; over 165,000 visitors a year

speyer_cathedral.when: begun 1030 under Conrad II, consecrated 1061; nave rebuilt about 1090 under Henry IV; last imperial burial 1308; UNESCO 1981
speyer_cathedral.site: the Rhine at Speyer, an imperial city — a dynasty that wants a burial church puts it where the empire is administered from
speyer_cathedral.size: the largest Romanesque church left standing; a groin vault of square bays over the nave; a crypt of 850 m² holding eight rulers of three dynasties

serpent_mound.when: built about 300 BCE on 2014 and 2019 radiocarbon dating, rebuilt or repaired around 1100 CE; whose it is remains argued
serpent_mound.who: Adena on the radiocarbon dates; Fort Ancient on the iconography, which is Brad Lepper's case
serpent_mound.site: a ridge above Brush Creek in Ohio, on the rim of a meteorite impact crater — and a figure this flat can only be read from above, which is not a viewpoint anyone who built it had
serpent_mound.size: 411 m long, 6.7 to 7.3 m wide, 23 cm to 91 cm high; the head aligned to the summer solstice sunset and the tail to the winter solstice sunrise; no burials in it

ciudad_perdida.site: a ridge in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta under dense jungle — steep enough that the city is terraces and stairs rather than streets, and hidden enough to be lost for centuries
ciudad_perdida.size: 169 terraces, tiled roads, several small circular plazas, and 1,200 stone steps up

pingyao.who: Ming and Qing Pingyao, and the draft banks that ran out of it
pingyao.site: the Shanxi plain on the trade routes north — a town whose business was moving other people's money needed walls more than most
pingyao.size: walls 12 m high and 6,163 m round enclosing 2.25 km², with 72 watchtowers and over 3,000 battlements; about 4,000 shops and residences of the 17th–19th centuries

luang_prabang.when: UNESCO listing covers 33 of its 58 villages
luang_prabang.who: the Lao royal capital, and the French after it
luang_prabang.site: the peninsula where the Nam Khan meets the Mekong — a town that cannot spread sideways puts everything on one strip

nelsons_dockyard.when: dockyard from 1725; Nelson stationed 1784–87; main construction 1785–94; abandoned by the Royal Navy 1889; restoration from 1951, reopened 1961
nelsons_dockyard.who: the Royal Navy, then the Society of the Friends of English Harbour
nelsons_dockyard.site: English Harbour on the south of Antigua — a hurricane hole that also looks out at the neighbouring islands, which is both halves of what a naval base needs
nelsons_dockyard.size: a capstan house for careening, a stone storehouse, and a sail loft of 1797; the only continuously working Georgian dockyard in the world

fatehpur_sikri.site: a ridge in Sikri with no dependable water — which is the one thing a capital cannot do without, and the reason it lasted fourteen years
fatehpur_sikri.size: built in red sandstone with post-and-lintel construction; the Buland Darwaza 54 m from the ground

qutb_minar.when: begun 1199 under Qutb ud-Din Aibak, completed about 1220 by Iltutmish; lightning 1369, earthquake 1803, restored 1828; UNESCO 1993
qutb_minar.who: Qutb ud-Din Aibak and Iltutmish, built by Hindu labourers under Muslim supervision
qutb_minar.site: Delhi, beside the first mosque built there — a victory tower is put where the victory is being announced
qutb_minar.size: 72.5 m in five storeys, 14.3 m across at the base and 2.7 m at the top, about 379 steps; the tallest brick minaret in the world

mahabodhi.when: the present structure 5th–6th century CE, on a site venerated since about 250 BCE under Ashoka; UNESCO June 2002
mahabodhi.who: the Gupta period, on Ashoka's foundation
mahabodhi.site: Bodh Gaya, beside the tree — the building is placed by a plant, and the plant is the reason anyone came
mahabodhi.size: a tower 55 m tall built entirely in brick; the Bodhi tree a direct descendant of the original

changdeokgung.when: built 1405; burned in the Imjin War in 1592 and rebuilt; UNESCO 1997
changdeokgung.site: a wooded hillside in Seoul that was fitted rather than flattened — the buildings follow the topography and the indigenous tree cover was kept
changdeokgung.size: the Huwon garden with over 160 species and more than 70 trees over 300 years old

plain_of_jars.when: jars placed as early as 1240–660 BC; Site 1 used for secondary burial from the 8th to 13th centuries CE; bombed 1964–69; UNESCO 2019
plain_of_jars.who: unknown; and then the United States Air Force
plain_of_jars.site: the Xiangkhoang plateau, where the stone was not — the jars at Site 1 came from a quarry eight kilometres away and others from about 100 km
plain_of_jars.size: 129 sites confirmed and over 2,100 jars documented, 1 to 3 m tall and up to 14 tonnes; an estimated 270 million cluster bomblets dropped, about 80 million unexploded

wat_phra_kaew.when: begun 1783; the Emerald Buddha installed February–March 1785
wat_phra_kaew.who: Rama I, and every king since who has changed the robes
wat_phra_kaew.site: inside the Grand Palace in Bangkok — a state shrine is put where the state is, not where the pilgrims are
wat_phra_kaew.size: the image about 66 cm tall; the gold garments changed three times a year at the turn of the seasons

Blue and John Crow Mountains — natural
central_asia: Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi — tomb
